analysis.one_liner: Offers House candidates full public campaign financing in exchange for running on small donations only.
analysis.headline: The bill won a voice-vote committee report in December 2010 but was never scheduled for a House floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Elections Now Act would have created a voluntary public financing system for House campaigns. A candidate who gathered enough small donations from state residents (at least $50,000 total, with contributions between $5 and $100 from a set number of residents) would qualify for a public allocation plus a 400% match on small-dollar contributions, in exchange for refusing all other campaign money, joining public debates, and returning unspent funds. The fund would be paid for mostly by diverting 10% of proceeds from auctions of recovered broadcast spectrum, plus FEC civil penalties and voluntary contributions.
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates without access to wealthy donors or expensive donor networks — challengers, first-time candidates, and candidates from less wealthy backgrounds — plus voters, who get more competitive elections, mandatory public debates, and fuller electronic disclosure of campaign reports. The bill's stated aim is to reduce the influence of large contributors over House members.

how_it_helps.text: Certified candidates get a public allocation (40% of a base amount for primaries, 60% for generals) plus a 400% match on qualifying small-dollar contributions, funded from spectrum auction proceeds rather than their own fundraising networks.

Participating candidates must refuse all contributions except small qualifying donations, may not spend personal or family funds, and must take part in at least one primary and two general-election public debates.

The bill's findings state that private campaign financing creates conflicts of interest, makes members accountable to major contributors, and discourages competitive elections; the program is designed to counter that by making candidates financially viable through many small donors.
All federal campaign filings would go directly to the FEC in electronic form, and the FEC would have to post them publicly within 24 hours instead of 48.
An oversight board of five presidentially appointed nonpartisan members — with registered lobbyists barred — would administer the program and audit at least a third of participating candidates.

analysis.who_pays: The program is funded mainly by redirecting 10% of proceeds from auctions of recovered broadcast spectrum away from the Digital Television Transition and Public Safety Fund, plus a share of FEC civil penalties and voluntary contributions — public money that would otherwise serve other purposes. Political party committees face tighter limits on coordinated spending with participating candidates, and taxpayers bear the administrative cost of the new oversight board and FEC auditing duties.

drawbacks.text: The program is entirely voluntary: wealthy self-funded candidates and campaigns bankrolled by large outside donors can simply decline to participate and outspend a participating candidate, a concern that grew sharply in the post-Citizens United spending environment of 2010.

The 400% match on small contributions is expensive relative to the money it replaces; the fund's main revenue source — 10% of spectrum auction proceeds — would come at the expense of the Digital Television Transition and Public Safety Fund, so public money is diverted from another public purpose.

Because participation is optional and the bill covers only House candidates, it would leave Senate races, presidential campaigns, and non-participating House campaigns financed exactly as before, limiting the reform's reach.
The base allocations are pegged to 80% of what winning House candidates spent in recent cycles, so the program's cost rises automatically as campaign spending climbs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For voters, the benefits are substantial: a real alternative to campaign finance built on large checks, mandatory debates, and faster public disclosure, at a cost measured in tens of millions from spectrum revenue rather than broad tax increases. The design is stronger than some public financing programs because qualifying depends on demonstrating broad small-donor support, not just accepting a lump sum. Its main weaknesses are voluntariness — leaving big-money campaigns untouched — and the fact that it addresses House races only. On balance the bill would shift influence from concentrated donors toward ordinary constituents, and the cost is modest relative to the federal budget.

outcome.mechanism: The House Administration Committee passed it on a voice vote and reported it in late December 2010, and it was placed on the House calendar, but the session ended three days later without leadership ever bringing it to the floor for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. John Larson introduced the bill on September 14, 2010, with 11 original cosponsors including two Republicans (Reps. Walter Jones and Todd Platts); it drew 18 cosponsors in total, 16 of 253 House Democrats and 2 of 178 House Republicans.
The House Administration Committee ordered the bill reported by voice vote on September 23, 2010, and formally reported it on December 21, 2010, as House Report 111-691.

The House Energy and Commerce Committee, which shared jurisdiction over the broadcasting provisions, was granted an extension through December 22, 2010, and was then discharged, clearing the bill for possible floor consideration.
On December 22, 2010, the bill was placed on the Union Calendar (Calendar No. 410), the step before floor action — but no floor vote ever came, and the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The private big-dollar fundraising system stayed intact: candidates who rely on large contributors and the donors who give to them kept the influence the bill would have diluted. House members never had to choose between the program and their existing donor networks, and party committees kept full coordinated-spending flexibility.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large donors and the existing fundraising system

for.name: Rep. John B. Larson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Elections Now Act in the House and recruited cosponsors across both parties.

for.name: House Committee on Administration
for.role: Committee with jurisdiction over election law (Chair: Rep. Robert Brady, D-PA)
for.what_they_did: Held a markup on September 23, 2010, ordered the bill reported by voice vote, and formally reported it to the House on December 21, 2010.

for.name: Fair Elections Now coalition (Public Campaign and allied reform groups)
for.role: Advocacy coalition for public campaign financing
for.what_they_did: Ran a multi-year public campaign urging Congress to pass Fair Elections Now legislation.

against.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote; it sat on the Union Calendar from December 22, 2010 until the Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

sides.party_line_note: Support came almost entirely from Democrats — 16 of 253 House Democrats versus 2 of 178 Republicans — and the committee reported it on a voice vote, but the bill never reached a floor vote where party lines could be counted.

industries.industry: Large campaign donors, lobbying firms, and joint fundraising PACs
industries.note: Participating candidates could accept nothing beyond small qualifying donations, eliminating the access that large checks buy, and joint fundraising committees with non-candidate committees would be banned. Because participation is voluntary, the system would have applied only to candidates who opted in.

Public allocations pegged to historical winning-candidate spending would still be spent heavily on television ads, so ad revenue would largely continue; mandatory debates could shift some spending toward free airtime exposure. Spectrum-auction proceeds that partly fund the program come from broadcasters' returned spectrum.

The bill tightens the limit on coordinated party spending with participating candidates, capping it at 10% of the candidate's general-election allocation, but only for candidates who join the program.
